title: Continuity of care: absences, coverage and a professional will
summary: Clients can be harmed when a clinician becomes unavailable without a plan, whether for a vacation, illness, a move or death. Codes ask clinicians to plan ahead so that care is not abandoned: arrange coverage, tell clients how to reach help, and name in a professional will a trusted colleague who can contact clients, keep records safe and arrange referrals. This page is information, not legal advice.
keyPoints: Codes ask you to plan for interruptions of care from illness, death, unavailability or relocation, and to provide for orderly transfer when you leave a job or practice (APA Standards 3.12 and 10.09; ACA Standard C.2.h; NASW Standard 1.17).
Planned absences: tell clients in advance, name a covering clinician, and give clear crisis instructions, including 988 and local emergency numbers, in your voicemail and away messages.
A professional will names an executor or records custodian, explains how to reach your schedule, client contacts, records and passwords, and includes notification letters and referral lists.
The custodian must protect records under privacy law and keep them for the period your state requires. Some boards ask to be told who holds your records.
Ending services: codes treat ending without notice or referral as abandonment, except when you are threatened or the client stops coming. Give notice and referrals when you can.
whatToDo: Write a coverage plan for planned absences and update voicemail and away messages with crisis numbers.
Draft a professional will naming a custodian, and keep access instructions secure and current.
Tell clients in your consent documents how care continues if you are suddenly unavailable.
Review the plan each year and whenever your practice changes.
Consult your licensing board and a healthcare attorney about record custody, retention and notice rules in your state.
questions: If I could not work tomorrow, who would tell my clients, and how?
Does my away message tell a client in crisis exactly what to do?
Can my custodian reach my records and contacts without breaking privacy rules?
How long must my records be kept, and who pays for that?
